Hard times

Not doing what you really love

Feeling that life is slipping away on something that does not fulfil you is common. What research says about calling, passion and meaning.

Many people spend most of the day in a job they did not fully choose or that no longer fulfils them, and feel that what really matters to them is left for "some day". That gap between what one does and what one would like to do can bring frustration, apathy and the feeling of living a borrowed life.

What we regret most

Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec found that in the short term we regret more what we did wrong, but in the long term the things we did not do weigh more heavily: studies never started, trips never taken, callings put on hold. It is worth bearing in mind, without letting it become a new source of pressure.

"Follow your passion" is not everything

A much-repeated piece of advice is to find your passion and devote yourself to it. Studies by Paul O'Keefe, Carol Dweck and Gregory Walton suggest that believing passion is "found" ready-made leads people to give up when difficulties appear. Passion, instead, usually develops over time, as one becomes competent at something and sees that what one does matters to others.

Changing without leaping into the void

It is not always possible or wise to drop everything. Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton described job crafting: small changes people make to their tasks, their work relationships or how they understand their job to give it more meaning. In their study, some hospital cleaners saw themselves as part of patient care and did more than their role required.

What tends to help

  • Clarifying values. Asking what kind of person you want to be and what you want to matter, beyond your job title.
  • Testing on a small scale. A course, volunteering or a side project let you check whether something is as appealing as you imagine.
  • Making room for what matters outside work. Meaning does not have to come only from employment.
  • Planning a change step by step if you decide to make the leap, with a financial cushion and support.

References

  1. Gilovich, T. y Medvec, V. H. (1995). The experience of regret: what, when, and why. Psychological Review, 102(2), 379–395.
  2. O'Keefe, P. A., Dweck, C. S. y Walton, G. M. (2018). Implicit theories of interest: finding your passion or developing it? Psychological Science, 29(10), 1653–1664.
  3. Wrzesniewski, A. y Dutton, J. E. (2001). Crafting a job: revisioning employees as active crafters of their work. Academy of Management Review, 26(2), 179–201.
